disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation) is characterized by developmentally inappropriate levels of motor activity, impulsivity, and difficulty inhibiting responses, with comparatively fewer or less prominent inattentive symptoms. Individuals often present with restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, interrupting others, and acting without considering consequences, which must cause impairment in at least two settings and be present for a prolonged period. In adults, the clinical picture may shift from overt hyperactivity toward inner restlessness and chronic impulsive decision-making, often impacting work performance, relationships, and safety. It is distinguished from anxiety disorders, bipolar spectrum conditions, and personality disorders by its early neurodevelopmental origins, pervasive pattern across contexts, and lack of sustained mood episodes, with symptoms typically fluctuating in intensity depending on demands rather than appearing episodically.

narrative.personality: He is a pragmatic, mechanically gifted tinkerer with a competitive streak, an intense focus on hands-on projects, and a tendency to push himself late into the night on hobbies.
narrative.stressor: About two and a half years ago, Darrin was promoted into a role that required more desk-based planning, vendor coordination, and safety meetings in addition to his usual hands-on maintenance work. The shift from primarily physical tasks to longer stretches of sitting, paperwork, and structured discussions exposed how hard it was for him to stay settled and focused when he wasn’t actively fixing something, leading to friction with a new supervisor who interpreted his constant movement and side projects as lack of professionalism. At the same time, he was taking on more complex home automation and car restoration work in his off-hours, often staying up late and juggling multiple unfinished projects, which began to spill over into fatigue, missed details on work orders, and tense conversations with his wife about his inability to “just sit still” with the family. Over the ensuing two years, repeated write-ups for not adhering to meeting protocols and complaints about his restlessness in training sessions, combined with worries that it might derail his goal of becoming a foreman, finally pushed him to seek a psychiatric evaluation at his wife’s urging and his own concern that something beyond simple stress was going on.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t sit still in meetings anymore—I’m always tapping or fidgeting and it’s starting to get me in trouble at work.”

narrative.personality: He is an energetic, curiosity-driven teacher who thrives on spontaneous, hands-on activities but struggles to rein in his own momentum and stay organized when demands pile up.
narrative.stressor: Roughly two years ago, Michael and his spouse welcomed their second child, which coincided with him taking on additional responsibilities at school, including leading STEM initiatives and coaching Little League. The combination of increased family duties, disrupted sleep, and extra roles that required long planning meetings and careful coordination made his long-standing restlessness and impulsive style far more problematic, as he found it harder to remain calmly present during family time and structured school activities. At home, his spouse became increasingly frustrated that he seemed unable to sit through meals, bedtime routines, or quiet evenings without pacing, fiddling with gadgets, or abruptly changing the topic or activity, which led to arguments about whether he was truly engaged with the family. At school, colleagues began commenting on his inability to stay seated during committees and his tendency to jump in before others finished speaking, and after a particularly tense parent conference where his constant movement was misread as disinterest, he agreed—at his spouse’s strong encouragement—to consult a psychiatrist to understand why his behavior was straining both his marriage and his professional relationships.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m constantly fidgeting and can’t seem to sit still at home or at school, and it’s starting to cause problems with my family and coworkers.”

narrative.personality: She is a warm, community-oriented technician who loves being busy with work, music, and volunteer activities, often overcommitting and staying constantly in motion.
narrative.stressor: Just over two years ago, Linda and her husband moved from a more urban area back to a rural community so she could pursue leadership opportunities in a regional telecom company while being closer to extended family. The move meant longer solo drives, more time managing jobs remotely, and a push from her employer to prepare for certification exams, all while she quickly plugged herself into choir, arts fairs, and church events, leaving almost no unstructured downtime. As the demands of studying, supervising more complex installations, and maintaining an active social calendar mounted, her long-standing tendency to stay perpetually active escalated into a pattern where she simply could not slow down, wearing out colleagues with her constant motion on job sites and overwhelming her own schedule to the point that she began missing key details and double-booking commitments. When a mentor gently suggested that her nonstop pace and difficulty ever sitting through planning meetings or rehearsals were holding her back from promotion and potentially affecting safety on complex jobs, she became worried enough about her future career and reputation in the community to seek a psychiatric assessment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’m always on the go and can’t ever just sit still, even when I know I need to slow down.”
